title: The many forms of the Word
source_text: Πάλιν τε αὖ ὁ λέγων· ἐπειδὴ θεῖον πνεῦμα ἦν ἐν σώματι, πάντως τι παραλλάττειν αὐτὸ τῶν λοιπῶν ἐχρῆν ἢ κατὰ μέγεθος ἢ φωνὴν ἢ ἀλκὴν ἢ κατάπληξιν ἢ πειθὼ πῶς οὐχ ἑώρα τὸ παραλλάττον τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ πρὸς τὸ τοῖς ὁρῶσι δυνατὸν καὶ διὰ τοῦτο χρήσιμον τοιοῦτο φαινόμενον, ὁποῖον ἔδει ἑκάστῳ βλέπεσθαι; καὶ οὐ θαυμαστὸν τὴν φύσει τρεπτὴν καὶ ἀλλοιωτὴν καὶ εἰς πάντα ἃ βούλεται ὁ δημιουργὸς ὕλην μεταβλητὴν καὶ πάσης ποιότητος, ἣν ὁ τεχνίτης βούλεται, δεκτικὴν, ὁτὲ μὲν ἔχειν ποιότητα, καθ᾿ ἣν λέγεται τό· „οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος οὐδὲ κάλλος,“ ὁτὲ δὲ οὕτως ἔνδοξον καὶ καταπληκτικὴν καὶ θαυμαστὴν, ὡς „ἐπὶ πρόσωπον“ πεσεῖν τοὺς θεατὰς τοῦ τηλικούτου κάλλους συνανελθόντας τῷ Ἰησοῦ· τρεῖς ἀποστόλους. ἀλλ᾿ ἐρεῖ ταῦτ᾿ εἶναι πλάσματα καὶ μύθων οὐδὲν διαφέροντα, ὡς καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ τῶν περὶ Ἰησοῦ παραδόξων. πρὸς τόδε (μὲν οὖν) διὰ πλειόνων ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων ἀπελογησάμεθα· ἔχει δέ τι καὶ μυστικώτερον ὁ λόγος, ἀπαγγέλλων τὰς τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διαφόρους μορφὰς φὰς ἀναφέρεσθαι ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ θείου λόγου φύσιν, οὐχ ὁμοίως φαινομένου τοῖς τε πολλοῖς καὶ τοῖς ἀκολουθεῖν αὐτῷ „εἰς ὑψηλὸν,“ ὃ ἀποδεδώκαμεν, „ὄρος“ δυναμένοις. τοῖς μὲν γὰρ ἔτι κάτω τυγχάνουσι καὶ μηδέπω ἐπὶ τὸ ἀναβαίνειν παρεσκευασμένοις ὁ λόγος „οὐκ ἔχει εἶδος οὐδὲ κάλλος“· τὸ γὰρ „εἶδος αὐτοῦ“ τοῖς τοιούτοις ἐστὶν „ἄτιμον καὶ ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς „ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων γεγενημένους λόγους, τροπικῶς ἐν τούτοις καλουμένους „υἱοὺς ἀνθρώπων.“ εἴποιμεν γὰρ ἂν πολλῷ ὡραιοτέρους φαίνεσθαι τοὺς τῶν φιλοσοφούντων λόγους, ὄντας „υἱοὺς ἀνθρώπων,“ παρὰ τὸν τοῖς πολλοῖς κηρυσσόμενον θεοῦ λόγον, ὃς ἐμφαίνει καὶ μωρίαν „κηρύγματος“· καὶ διὰ τὴν ἐμφαινομένην μωρίαν „τοῦ κηρύγματος“ λέγουσιν οἱ τοῦτο μόνον θεωροῦντες· „εἴδομεν αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος οὐδὲ κάλλος.“ τοῖς μέντοι (ἐκ τοῦ) ἀκολουθεῖν αὐτῷ δύναμιν ἀνειληφόσι πρὸς τὸ ἕπεσθαι καὶ ἀναβαίνοντι αὐτῷ „εἰς τὸ ὑψηλὸν ὄρος“ θειοτέραν μορφὴν ἔχει· ἣν βλέπουσιν, εἴ τις ἐστὶ „Πέτρος,“ χωρήσας τὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἐν αὑτῷ οἰκοδομὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου καὶ τοσαύτην ἕξιν ἀναλαβὼν, ὡς μηδεμίαν πύλην ᾅδου κατισχύσειν αὐτοῦ, ὑψωθέντος διὰ τὸν λόγον „ἐκ τῶν πυλῶν τοῦ θανάτου, ὅπως ἂν“ ἐξαγγείλῃ „πάσας τὰς αἰνέσεις“ τοῦ θεοῦ „ἐν ταῖς πύλαις τῆς θυγατρὸς Σιών“· καὶ εἴ τινες εἰσὶν ἐκ λόγων τὴν γένεσιν λαβόντες μεγαλοφώνων, οἵτινες οὐδὲν ἀποδέουσι νοητῆς „βροντῆς.“ <καὶ „τὰ ἱμάτια“ δὲ „αὐτοῦ“ κάτω ἄλλα ἐστὶν, οὐκ ἔστι „λευκὰ,“ οὐκ ἔστιν „ὡς τὸ φῶς“· ἐὰν ἀναβῇς „εἰς τὸ ὄρος τὸ ὑψηλὸν,“ ὄψει αὐτοῦ φῶς καὶ „τὰ ἱμάτια.“ „τὰ ἱμάτια“ τοῦ λόγου αἱ λέξεις εἰσὶ τῆς γραφῆς, ἔνδυμα τῶν θείων νοημάτων τὰ ῥήματά ἐστι ταῦτα. ὡς οὖν αὐτὸς κάτω ἀλλοῖος φαίνεται καὶ ἀναβὰς μεταμορφοῦται καὶ γίνεται „τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ὡς ὁ ἥλιος,“ οὕτω καὶ τὰ ἐνδύματα αὐτοῦ, οὕτω καὶ „τὰ ἱμάτια“· ὅταν δὲ ᾖς κάτω, οὐκ ἔστι λαμπρὰ, οὐκ ἔστι „λευκά“· ἐὰν δὲ ἀναβῇς, ὄψει τὸ κάλλος καὶ „τὸ φῶς“ τῶν ἱματίων, καὶ „τὸ πρόσωπον“ θαυμάσεις τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μεταμορφωθέν. ὅρα δὲ εἰ μὴ ὅμοιόν ἐστι καὶ ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος μαθεῖν. τὰ μὲν γὰρ περὶ τῆς γενέσεως αὐτοῦ, γενεαλογουμένου ἐξ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ „γεννωμένου ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυῒδ κατὰ σάρκα,“ „βίβλος“ ἐστὶ „γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ“· τὰ δὲ θειότερα καὶ μείζονα τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ λεχθησομένων ἂν καὶ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἀπαγγελλομένων φησὶν ὁ Ἰωάννης, ὡς ἄρα „οὐδὲ τὸν κόσμον οἶμαι χωρεῖν τὰ γραφόμενα βιβλία.“ τὸ γὰρ μὴ „χωρεῖν τὸν κόσμον τὰ γραφόμενα βιβλία“ οὐ διὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν γραμμάτων, ὥς τινες, ἐκδεκτέον, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ μέγεθος τῶν πραγμάτων· τοῦ μεγέθους τῶν πραγμάτων οὐ μόνον οὐ δυναμένου γράφεσθαι ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ διὰ γλώσσης σαρκίνης ἀπαγγέλλεσθαι οὐδὲ ἐν διαλέκτοις καὶ φωναῖς ἀνθρωπίναις σημαίνεσθαι. ὅθεν καὶ Παῦλος, ἐπὰν μανθάνειν μέλλῃ τὰ θειότερα, ἔξω τοῦ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς περιγείου κόσμου γίνεται καὶ εἰς τρίτον οὐρανὸν ἁρπάζεται, ἵνα τὰ ἐκεῖθεν „ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα“ ἀκοῦσαι δυνηθῇ. τὰ γὰρ ἐνθάδε λαλούμενα καὶ λόγος εἶναι θεοῦ νομιζόμενα, τοῦ λόγου σαρκωθέντος καὶ καθὸ „θεός“ ἐστι „πρὸς τὸν θεὸν“ ἑαυτὸν κενοῦντος, ἀπαγγέλλεται. διόπερ τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ λόγον ἐπὶ „γῆς, ἐπεὶ ἄνθρωπος γέγονεν, ἀνθρώπινον βλέπομεν· ἀεὶ γὰρ ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς „ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο,“ ἵνα κατασκηνώσῃ „ἐν ἡμῖν“· ἀλλ᾿ ἐὰν εἰς „τὸ στῆθος“ τοῦ σαρκωθέντος λόγου ἀνακλιθῶμεν καὶ ἀνιόντι αὐτῷ „εἰς τὸ ὑψηλον ὄρος“ ἀκολουθῆσαι δυνηθῶμεν, ἐροῦμεν τό· „εἴδομεν τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ“· τάχα μέν τινων καὶ ἑτέρων παρὰ τοὺς ἀνακλιθέντας ἐπὶ τοῦ στήθους αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀκολουθήσαντας αὐτῷ „εἰς τὸ ὄρος τὸ ὑψηλὸν“ λεξόντων τό· „εἴδομεν τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ,“ οὐκέτι δὲ προσθησόντων τό· „δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρὸς. πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας“· Ἰωάννῃ γὰρ καὶ τοῖς ὁμοίοις πρέπουσα αὕτη ἡ φωνή. καὶ καθ᾿ ἑτέραν δὲ ὑψηλοτέραν διήγησιν οἱ δυνηθέντες τοῖς ἴχνεσιν Ἰησοῦ κατακολουθεῖν, ἀναβαίνοντος καὶ μεταμορφουμένου ἀπὸ τῆς ἐπὶ γῆς ὄψεως, ὄψονται αὐτοῦ τὴν μεταμόρφωσιν καθ᾿ ἑκάστην γραφήν· οἱονεὶ τοῦ μὲν τοῖς πολλοῖς φαινομένου Ἰησοῦ τῆς προχείρου λέξεως ὄντος, τοῦ δὲ „εἰς ὄρος ὑψηλὸν“ ἀνιόντος καὶ μεταμορφουμένου σφόδρα ὀλίγοις τῶν μαθητῶν καὶ τοῖς ἀκολουθῆσαι εἰς τὰ ὑψηλὰ δεδυνημένοις τοῦ ἀνωτάτου καὶ ὑψηλοτάτου νοῦ, περιέχοντος λόγια τῆς „ἐν μυστηρίῳ“ ἀποκεκρυμμένης σοφίας, „ἣν προώρισεν ὁ θεὸς πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων εἰς δόξαν“ τῶν δικαίων αὐτοῦ.> ἀλλὰ πόθεν Κέλσῳ καὶ τοῖς ἐχθροῖς τοῦ θείου λόγου καὶ μὴ φιλαλήθως τὰ χριστιανισμοῦ ἐξετάσασιν εἰδέναι τὸ βούλημα τῶν διαφόρων τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μορφῶν; ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω καὶ ἡλικιῶν, καὶ εἴ τι τῶν πρὸ τοῦ παθεῖν αὐτῷ πεπραγμένων καὶ τῶν μετὰ τὸ ἀναστῆναι ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν.
pass_a_gloss: And again the one saying: 'Since a divine spirit was in a body, it must altogether differ somewhat from the rest, either in size or voice or strength (ἀλκή) or striking awe (κατάπληξις) or persuasion (πειθώ)', how did he not see the differing (τὸ παραλλάττον) of his body relative to what was possible (δυνατόν) for the beholders, and for this reason useful (χρήσιμον), appearing such as it was needful to be seen by each? And [it is] not wonderful that matter (ὕλη), by nature turnable (τρεπτήν) and alterable (ἀλλοιωτήν) and changeable (μεταβλητήν) into all things the craftsman (δημιουργός) wills, and receptive (δεκτικήν) of every quality (ποιότης) the artisan (τεχνίτης) wills, at one time has a quality according to which is said 'he had no form nor beauty', at another so glorious (ἔνδοξον) and astonishing (καταπληκτικήν) and wonderful that the beholders (θεατάς) of so great beauty, who had gone up with (συνανελθόντας) Jesus, three apostles, fell 'upon [their] face (πρόσωπον)'. But he will say these are fictions (πλάσματα) and differ nothing from myths (μύθων), as also the rest of the marvels (παραδόξων) about Jesus. To this we have defended (ἀπελογησάμεθα) at greater length in the parts before these; but the account (λόγος) has something more mystical (μυστικώτερον), announcing the different forms (μορφάς) of Jesus to be referred to the nature (φύσιν) of the divine Word (θείου λόγου), not appearing alike to the many and to those able to follow him 'onto a high', as we have rendered (ἀποδεδώκαμεν), 'mountain'. For to those still below and not yet prepared for going up, the Word 'has no form nor beauty'; for 'his form' to such is 'dishonoured and failing beside' the words (λόγους) become/begotten by men, figuratively (τροπικῶς) called in these 'sons of men'. For we might say that the words of those philosophising appear much more comely (ὡραιοτέρους), being 'sons of men', beside the Word of God proclaimed to the many, which shows (ἐμφαίνει) also foolishness (μωρία) 'of proclamation (κηρύγματος)'; and because of the apparent foolishness 'of the proclamation' those beholding this alone say: 'We saw him and he had no form nor beauty.' But to those who from following him have taken up power (δύναμιν) toward keeping pace (ἕπεσθαι) even with him going up 'onto the high mountain', he has a more divine form (θειοτέραν μορφήν); which they see, if anyone is a 'Peter', having made room for (χωρήσας) the building (οἰκοδομήν) of the church (ἐκκλησία) in himself from the Word and having taken up such a habit/state (ἕξιν) that no gate of Hades (πύλην ᾅδου) will prevail against (κατισχύσειν) him, lifted up (ὑψωθέντος) through the Word 'from the gates of death, so that he may' declare 'all the praises (αἰνέσεις)' of God 'in the gates of the daughter of Zion'; and if there are some having taken birth (γένεσιν) from words of great voice (μεγαλοφώνων), who fall short (ἀποδέουσι) in nothing of intelligible (νοητῆς) 'thunder (βροντῆς)'. <And 'his garments (ἱμάτια)' below are other: they are not 'white (λευκά)', not 'as the light (φῶς)'; if you go up 'onto the high mountain' you will see his light and 'the garments'. 'The garments' of the Word are the wordings (λέξεις) of scripture (γραφή); these utterances (ῥήματα) are a clothing (ἔνδυμα) of the divine thoughts (νοημάτων). As then he himself below appears other (ἀλλοῖος) and having gone up is transformed (μεταμορφοῦται) and 'his face becomes as the sun', so also his clothes, so also 'the garments'; when you are below they are not bright (λαμπρά), not 'white'; if you go up, you will see the beauty and 'the light' of the garments, and you will marvel at 'the face' of Jesus transformed. See whether it is not similar also to learn in the gospels about the Saviour (σωτήρ). For the things about his birth (γενέσεως), being traced in genealogy (γενεαλογουμένου) from Abraham and 'born of the seed of David according to the flesh (σάρκα)', are 'a book (βίβλος) of the genesis (γενέσεως) of Jesus Christ'; but the more divine and greater of the things that would be said about him and announced by him John says, that 'not even the world, I suppose (οἶμαι), would contain (χωρεῖν) the books being written'. For the world's not containing the books being written is to be taken (ἐκδεκτέον) not because of the multitude of letters (γραμμάτων), as some [say], but because of the greatness (μέγεθος) of the matters (πραγμάτων); the greatness of the matters not only being unable to be written but not even to be announced through a fleshly tongue (γλώσσης σαρκίνης) nor signified in human dialects (διαλέκτοις) and sounds (φωναῖς). Whence also Paul, when he is about to learn the more divine things, comes to be outside the earthly (περιγείου) world in our region and is snatched (ἁρπάζεται) into the third heaven, so that he may be able to hear the 'unspeakable utterances (ἄρρητα ῥήματα)' from there. For the things spoken here and thought to be word of God are announced, the Word having been made flesh (σαρκωθέντος) and, in so far as (καθό) he is 'God' 'with (πρός) God', emptying (κενοῦντος) himself. Therefore we see the Word of God upon 'earth', since he has become man (ἄνθρωπος), as human (ἀνθρώπινον); for always in the scriptures 'the Word became flesh', so that he may tabernacle (κατασκηνώσῃ) 'among us'; but if we recline (ἀνακλιθῶμεν) upon 'the breast (στῆθος)' of the incarnate Word and are able to follow him going up 'onto the high mountain', we shall say: 'We saw his glory'; perhaps indeed some others besides those who reclined on his breast and followed him 'onto the high mountain' will say 'We saw his glory', but will no longer add (προσθησόντων) 'glory as of an only-begotten (μονογενοῦς) from a father, full of grace (χάριτος) and truth (ἀληθείας)'; for to John and those like him this voice is fitting (πρέπουσα). And according to another, higher explanation (διήγησιν), those able to follow closely in the footprints (ἴχνεσιν) of Jesus, going up and being transformed from the appearance (ὄψεως) on earth, will see his transformation (μεταμόρφωσιν) in each scripture; as though the Jesus appearing to the many were the ready-to-hand wording (προχείρου λέξεως), and the one going up 'onto a high mountain' and transformed before very few of the disciples and those able to follow to the heights were the uppermost and highest sense (νοῦ), containing oracles (λόγια) of the wisdom (σοφίας) hidden (ἀποκεκρυμμένης) 'in a mystery (μυστηρίῳ)', 'which God foreordained (προώρισεν) before the ages (αἰώνων) for glory' of his righteous ones (δικαίων).> But whence [is it] for Celsus and the enemies of the divine Word, and those not examining in a truth-loving way (φιλαλήθως) the things of Christianity, to know the intent (βούλημα) of the different forms of Jesus? And I say also of ages (ἡλικιῶν), and whatever of the things done by him before suffering (παθεῖν) and after rising (ἀναστῆναι) from the dead.
pass_b_english: Again, the man who says, “Since a divine spirit was in a body, it surely ought to have differed somewhat from the rest, in size or voice or strength or power to astonish or persuasiveness”: how did he not see that his body differed according to what the beholders were able to receive, and was useful for that very reason, appearing such as it had to be seen by each? And it is not surprising that matter, which by nature is mutable and alterable, can be changed into whatever the Creator wills, and can receive every quality the Craftsman wills, should at one time have the quality of which it is said, “He had no form nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2), and at another time one so glorious and awe-inspiring and wonderful that those who beheld such great beauty, the three apostles who had gone up with Jesus, fell “on their faces” (Matthew 17:6).

But he will say that these are fictions, no different from myths, like the rest of the wonders told about Jesus. We have already answered this at length in what came before. But the account also holds something more mystical: it declares that the different forms of Jesus refer to the nature of the divine Word, who does not appear in the same way to the many and to those able to follow him “onto a high mountain,” as we have explained it.

For to those who are still below and not yet ready to go up, the Word “has no form nor beauty”; for to such people “his form” is “without honour, and falls short compared with” the words that men have brought forth, which are figuratively called “sons of men” in this passage (Isaiah 53:2–3). For we might say that the words of the philosophers, which are “sons of men,” appear far more comely than the Word of God preached to the many, which also shows a “foolishness of preaching” (1 Corinthians 1:21); and because of the “foolishness of the preaching” that shows in it, those who look at this alone say, “We saw him, and he had no form nor beauty.”

But to those who, by following him, have received the power to keep up with him even as he goes up “onto the high mountain,” he has a more divine form. They see it, if anyone is a “Peter,” who has made room within himself for the building of the Church by the Word and has reached so firm a state that no gate of Hades will prevail against him (Matthew 16:18), since he has been lifted up, because of the Word, “from the gates of death, that he may” declare “all the praises” of God “in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Psalm 9:13–14); and they see it, if there are any who have received their birth from words of a mighty voice, and fall in no way short of a “thunder” that the mind perceives (Mark 3:17).

And “his garments” are different below: they are not “white,” they are not “as the light” (Matthew 17:2). If you go up “onto the high mountain,” you will see his light and “his garments.” The “garments” of the Word are the wording of Scripture; these words are the clothing of the divine thoughts. So as he himself appears different below, and when he has gone up is transfigured and “his face” becomes “like the sun” (Matthew 17:2), so too his clothing, so too “his garments.” When you are below, they are not bright, they are not “white”; but if you go up, you will see the beauty and “the light” of the garments, and you will marvel at “the face” of Jesus transfigured.

Consider whether it is not the same with what we learn about the Saviour in the Gospels too. For what concerns his birth, as his descent is traced from Abraham and he is “born of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3), is “the book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1). But of the more divine and greater things that might be said about him and that he himself declared, John says that “not even the world, I suppose, could contain the books that would be written” (John 21:25). For the saying that “the world could not contain the books that would be written” is to be understood not, as some take it, of the number of the writings, but of the greatness of the matters; for the greatness of the matters not only cannot be written down, but cannot even be told by a tongue of flesh, nor expressed in human languages and sounds.

That is why Paul too, when he was about to learn the more divine things, came to be outside this earthly world of ours and was caught up into the third heaven, so that he might be able to hear the “unspeakable words” there (2 Corinthians 12:2–4). For what is spoken here, and is held to be the word of God, is told now that the Word has become flesh and, in respect of his being “God” “with God” (John 1:1), empties himself (Philippians 2:7). That is why we see the Word of God on earth as human, since he has become man; for in the Scriptures “the Word” is always becoming “flesh,” that he may dwell “among us” (John 1:14).

But if we lean back on “the breast” of the Word made flesh (John 13:25), and are able to follow him as he goes up “onto the high mountain,” we shall say, “We saw his glory” (John 1:14). Perhaps some others too, besides those who leaned on his breast and followed him “onto the high mountain,” will say, “We saw his glory,” but will not go on to add, “glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14); for this utterance befits John and those like him.

And by another, higher interpretation, those who have been able to follow close in the footsteps of Jesus as he goes up and is transfigured from his earthly appearance will see his transfiguration in each Scripture. It is as though the Jesus who appears to the many were the plain wording, while the Jesus who goes up “onto a high mountain” and is transfigured before very few of the disciples, and before those who have been able to follow to the heights, were the highest and loftiest sense, which holds the oracles of the wisdom hidden “in a mystery,” “which God foreordained before the ages for the glory” of his righteous ones (1 Corinthians 2:7).

But how could Celsus, and the enemies of the divine Word, who have not examined Christianity with a love of truth, know the meaning of the different forms of Jesus? And I mean also of his different ages, and of whatever he did before he suffered and after he rose from the dead.

choices.choice: Celsus’s quotation here repeats 6.75 with a shorter list (no ‘beauty’); translated as given. ὁ δημιουργός / ὁ τεχνίτης: Origen means God, so ‘Creator’ and ‘Craftsman’ are capitalised. The copy-text has a dittography μορφὰς φὰς; read μορφάς. ὃ ἀποδεδώκαμεν (‘as we have explained/rendered it’) points to Origen’s earlier reading of the high mountain (compare 2.64-65, 4.16 and 6.68); not cited. ‘Peter’ and the Church built in him allude to Matthew 16:16-18 (πύλαι ᾅδου οὐ κατισχύσουσιν αὐτῆς); Origen applies it to every ‘Peter’. ‘From the gates of death ... daughter of Zion’ is LXX Psalm 9:14-15 = English Psalm 9:13-14 (Origen changes first person to third). ‘Words of a mighty voice ... thunder’ alludes to the sons of thunder, James and John (Mark 3:17); νοητή βροντή rendered ‘a thunder that the mind perceives’. The long passage from καὶ τὰ ἱμάτια to τῶν δικαίων αὐτοῦ is enclosed in angle brackets in the copy-text; it is translated in full and its textual status should be checked against Koetschau’s apparatus. Garments ‘white as the light’ and ‘face like the sun’: Matthew 17:2. βίβλος γενέσεως rendered ‘the book of the genealogy’ (Matthew 1:1), keeping the link with γενεαλογουμένου. John 21:25 is cited loosely by Origen (οὐδὲ τὸν κόσμον οἶμαι χωρεῖν τὰ γραφόμενα βιβλία). ‘Third heaven’ and ‘unspeakable words’ are 2 Corinthians 12:2-4. καθὸ θεός ἐστι πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἑαυτὸν κενοῦντος combines John 1:1 with Philippians 2:7; the sense of καθό (‘in respect of his being God with God’) is condensed and may be read more than one way. ἐπὶ „γῆς is marked as a quotation in the copy-text, possibly an echo of Baruch 3:38 (LXX 3:37, ‘he appeared on earth’); uncertain, so not cited inline. ἀεὶ γὰρ ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο rendered ‘in the Scriptures the Word is always becoming flesh’ to carry the force of ἀεί.
